subject: ss
title: Rights, Amendments, and Citizenship
objectives: You will explain why the Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution and identify the main protection in each of the first ten amendments.
You will distinguish civil liberties from civil rights, explain why constitutional rights have limits, and describe how incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to the states.
You will describe how the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments changed the Constitution after the Civil War, and how the 17th, 19th, 24th, and 26th Amendments expanded voting.
You will explain how a person becomes a U.S. citizen and sort the rights and responsibilities of citizenship into citizens-only, required, and voluntary.
You will answer GED-style social studies questions using amendment texts, Supreme Court opinions, tables, and charts.

slides.title: Rights, Amendments, and Citizenship
slides.board:
Week 3 Social Studies: Rights, Amendments, and Citizenship

Today you will:

  • Explain why the Bill of Rights was added and name the main protection in each amendment
  • Tell civil liberties from civil rights and explain why rights have limits
  • Describe the Civil War amendments and the amendments that expanded the vote
  • Explain how a person becomes a citizen and sort duties into required and voluntary
  • Answer GED-style questions with amendment texts, court opinions, and charts

Plan: Warm-up → six big ideas → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 3. Last week we studied how the Constitution builds the government. This week we study what the Constitution protects: your rights. Amendment texts and Supreme Court opinions are some of the most common documents on the GED Social Studies test, and the questions usually describe a real-life situation and ask which right applies. By the end of today you should be able to hear a situation and name the amendment behind it, and then prove it with the words of the text.
ask: Name one right you believe you have as a person living in the United States. Where do you think that right is written down? (Expected: any answer, such as free speech or a fair trial. Use it to point out that most of these rights are in the amendments we study today.)

slides.title: Warm-up: Review of the Constitution
slides.board:
Week 2 review. Answer each one.

  1. Which branch of government interprets the laws, and which article creates it?
  2. The President vetoes a bill. What fraction of each house of Congress must vote to override the veto?
  3. Delegated, reserved, or concurrent? (a) coining money (b) issuing driver’s licenses (c) collecting taxes
  4. Article V: an amendment is usually proposed by ___ of both houses of Congress and ratified by ___ of the states.
steps: 1. The judicial branch (the Supreme Court and lower courts), created by Article III.
2. Two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate.
3. (a) Delegated (national only) (b) Reserved (states, under the 10th Amendment) (c) Concurrent (both levels)
4. Proposed by two-thirds of both houses; ratified by three-fourths of the states (38 of 50).

notes.say: These four questions review last week and set up today. Give the student about three minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. Question 3(b) uses the 10th Amendment, and question 4 is the amendment process, which is how every right we study today got into the Constitution. If the student misses one, take thirty seconds to re-teach it now; we build on all four.
ask: Why is it hard to amend the Constitution? (Expected: it takes two-thirds of both houses and three-fourths of the states, so it needs very wide support)
Which amendment reserves powers to the states? (Expected: the 10th)
notes.answer: 1. Judicial branch, Article III. 2. Two-thirds of both houses. 3. (a) delegated (b) reserved (c) concurrent. 4. Two-thirds; three-fourths (38 states).
notes.watch: On question 4, students often reverse the fractions. Say: "Congress proposes with two-thirds; the states ratify with three-fourths. The bigger fraction is the last step."

slides.title: Why a Bill of Rights?
slides.board:
The Constitution (1787) had no list of rights. The Anti-Federalists feared a strong national government would take away freedoms. Supporters promised to add a list.

  • James Madison drafted the amendments in 1789.
  • Ten were ratified in 1791: the Bill of Rights.
  • Key idea: it limits government. "Congress shall make no law…"
1st Amendment: five freedoms
Religion (no official church; free exercise) · Speech · Press · Assembly · Petition

notes.say: When the Constitution went to the states in 1787, it set up a powerful new national government but listed very few individual rights. The Anti-Federalists said that was dangerous: what stops this government from silencing critics or searching homes? To win ratification, supporters of the Constitution promised to add a list of rights. James Madison drafted the amendments in 1789, and the first ten were ratified in 1791. Notice the first words of the First Amendment: "Congress shall make no law." The Bill of Rights is a list of things the government may not do to you. The First Amendment protects five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. A petition is a formal request asking the government to fix a problem.
ask: Who does the Bill of Rights limit: the government or private people? (Expected: the government)
Name the five freedoms of the First Amendment. (Expected: religion, speech, press, assembly, petition)
notes.watch: Students mix up assembly (gathering together) and petition (a formal request to the government). Ask: "Are people gathering, or are they asking the government to do something?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Which Freedom?
slides.board:
"Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances."

Tenants collect 150 signatures asking the city to inspect their unsafe building and deliver them to city hall. Which phrase protects them?
steps: Step 1: Translate the situation. People are making a formal request asking the government to fix a problem.
Step 2: Rule out the near misses. They are not gathering (assembly), publishing (press), or practicing a religion (free exercise).
Step 3: Match the words. "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances" = ask the government to fix a complaint.
Answer: the right to petition, protected by the First Amendment.

notes.say: Model the habit we will use all day: first say in plain words what the people are doing, then find the phrase that matches. Underline "redress of grievances" and translate it: fixing a complaint. Point out that "abridging" means reducing or limiting; we will see that word again in the voting amendments.
ask: What would change in the story to make it an assembly question? (Expected: if the tenants gathered together, for example at a rally outside city hall)
notes.watch: Some students pick speech because the tenants are expressing an opinion. Speech is close, but the First Amendment names the exact action of asking the government for a fix: petition. The GED wants the most specific match.

slides.title: Follow the Case: Rights of the Accused
slides.board:
StageAmendmentMain protections
1. The search4thNo unreasonable searches and seizures; a warrant needs probable cause
2. Charges and questioning5thGrand jury; no double jeopardy; no forced self-incrimination; due process
3. The trial6thSpeedy, public trial; impartial jury; know the charges; face witnesses; a lawyer
4. The punishment8thNo excessive bail or fines; no cruel and unusual punishment

Also: 7th = jury in many civil (non-criminal) lawsuits.

notes.say: Four amendments protect people accused of crimes, and the easiest way to remember them is to follow a case in order. The search comes first: the Fourth Amendment says searches must be reasonable, and a warrant must be based on probable cause, a fact-based reason to believe evidence will be found. Next come the charges and questioning: the Fifth Amendment says you cannot be tried twice for the same crime after a verdict, which is double jeopardy, and you cannot be forced to testify against yourself, which is why people "plead the Fifth." Then the trial: the Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy, public trial, an impartial jury, and a lawyer. Last, the punishment: the Eighth Amendment bans excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishment.
ask: What is double jeopardy, and which amendment bans it? (Expected: being tried again for the same crime after a verdict; the 5th)
Which amendment guarantees a lawyer at trial? (Expected: the 6th)
notes.watch: The classic mistake: putting double jeopardy under the 6th Amendment because it involves a trial. Remind the student that the 5th Amendment holds three "no" rules: no double jeopardy, no forced self-incrimination, no loss of life, liberty, or property without due process.

slides.title: Worked Example: Maria on the Stand
slides.board:
Maria is on trial for theft. The judge orders her to take the witness stand and answer the prosecutor’s questions about the crime. Her lawyer objects.

Which amendment applies, and should the judge’s order stand?
steps: Step 1: Translate. The government is forcing an accused person to testify against herself.
Step 2: Find the stage. It happens at trial, but the protection is about being forced to be a witness against yourself, which is in the 5th, not the 6th.
Step 3: Quote the text. The 5th Amendment says no person "shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself."
Answer: The order violates the 5th Amendment protection against self-incrimination. Maria may choose not to testify.

notes.say: This example is built to catch the stage trick. The event happens at a trial, so students jump to the Sixth Amendment. But the right being violated is not about how the trial is run; it is about forcing a defendant to testify. That protection lives in the Fifth. Teach the student to name the right first, then the amendment.
ask: If the judge refused to let Maria have a lawyer, which amendment would that violate? (Expected: the 6th)
notes.watch: If the student says the 6th, ask: "What exactly is the government making her do?" Once they say "testify against herself," point to the Fifth Amendment text.

slides.title: We Do: Name the Amendment
slides.board:
1. Police search a man’s backpack on the street with no warrant, no emergency, and no permission.
  2. A woman is found not guilty of fraud. The prosecutor charges her again for the same fraud.
  3. A man is held in jail for three years without a trial, though he has asked for one.
  4. A court sentences a person to 20 years in prison for a $5 parking ticket.
steps: 1. 4th Amendment. A search with no warrant, no emergency, and no consent is unreasonable.
2. 5th Amendment. Being tried again for the same crime after a verdict is double jeopardy.
3. 6th Amendment. He is denied a speedy trial.
4. 8th Amendment. A punishment so far out of proportion to the offense is cruel and unusual.

notes.say: Do these together. For each one, have the student say the stage first (search, charges, trial, or punishment), then the amendment, then the words that prove it. Reveal each answer only after the student commits.
ask: For number 2: what stage is this, and what is the key phrase? (Expected: charges; "twice put in jeopardy")
For number 4: is the problem the trial or the punishment? (Expected: the punishment)
notes.watch: Number 3 tempts some students toward the 5th Amendment (due process). Due process is broad, but the 6th Amendment names the exact right: "a speedy and public trial." Always pick the most specific protection.

slides.title: Civil Liberties, Civil Rights, and Limits
slides.board:
Civil liberties
Freedoms the government may not take away
Freedom FROM government interference
Speech, religion, press, fair trial

Civil rights
Guarantees of equal treatment
Equal treatment UNDER the law
No discrimination by race, sex, religion, national origin

  • Rights have limits: no protection for true threats; Tinker (1969): schools may limit speech that would substantially disrupt school.
  • Incorporation: the 14th Amendment is used to apply most of the Bill of Rights to states and cities.

notes.say: These two terms sound alike, and the GED expects you to tell them apart. A civil liberty is a freedom the government may not take away: speech, religion, privacy from unreasonable searches, a fair trial. Think "freedom from government interference." A civil right is a guarantee of equal treatment, so people are not discriminated against because of race, sex, religion, national origin, or similar traits. Think "equal treatment under the law." Rights are not unlimited: courts balance your freedom against public safety and the rights of others. In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court said students keep free speech at school, but a school may limit speech that would substantially disrupt school. Finally, the Bill of Rights first limited only the national government. Starting in the 1920s, the Court used the 14th Amendment to apply most of it to state and local governments. That is incorporation, and it is why a city police officer must respect the Fourth Amendment.
ask: A restaurant refuses to serve a family because of their religion. Liberty or right? (Expected: civil right, unequal treatment)
Does free speech protect a true threat? (Expected: No; rights have limits)
notes.watch: Students sometimes say anything involving religion is a civil liberty. Ask the deciding question: "Is the government limiting a freedom, or is a group being treated unequally?" A business refusing service because of religion is unequal treatment, so it is a civil rights issue.

slides.title: Worked Example: Applying a Court Opinion
slides.board:
Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), majority opinion: students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." A ban cannot stand without a showing that the conduct would "materially and substantially interfere" with school discipline.

A school bans buttons that support a candidate for mayor. No button has caused any problem. Would the ban likely be upheld?
steps: Step 1: Find the rule. Students keep free expression, unless the school shows a substantial disruption.
Step 2: Check the facts. No button has caused a problem, and nothing suggests one would.
Step 3: Apply the rule to the facts. No showing of substantial disruption means the ban "cannot be sustained."
Answer: The ban would likely be struck down under Tinker. Buttons, like the armbands in Tinker, are symbolic speech.

notes.say: GED court-opinion questions almost always work this way: they give you the rule from the opinion and a new set of facts, and ask how the rule applies. Teach the three moves: find the rule, check the facts, apply. Point out that the Court protected armbands, which are not spoken or written words, so "speech" includes symbolic expression.
ask: What one fact would change the answer? (Expected: evidence that the buttons were causing, or would cause, a substantial disruption, such as fights)
notes.watch: Watch for students who answer from personal opinion ("schools should be allowed to set rules"). Bring them back: "What does the opinion say the school must show?"

slides.title: We Do: Liberty or Right?
slides.board:
Label each as a civil liberty or civil right issue.

  1. A state law bans a newspaper from criticizing the governor.
  2. A company refuses to hire qualified applicants because they are women.
  3. A hotel turns away guests because of their national origin.
  4. A city forbids one religious group from holding services in its own building.
steps: 1. Civil liberty. The government is limiting freedom of the press.
2. Civil right. A group is treated unequally because of sex (Civil Rights Act of 1964).
3. Civil right. Unequal treatment in a public accommodation because of national origin.
4. Civil liberty. The government is limiting the free exercise of religion.

notes.say: For each case, ask the student the deciding question out loud: "Is the government taking away a freedom, or is a group being treated unequally?" Then reveal. Point out that numbers 2 and 3 involve businesses, and the law that protects people there is the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
ask: In number 4, who is acting: the government or a business? (Expected: the government, the city)
notes.watch: Number 4 mentions a religious group, so some students call it a civil right. The key is that the government is restricting worship itself, which is a freedom (free exercise), so it is a civil liberty.

slides.title: The Civil War Amendments
slides.board:
AmendmentYearWhat it did
13th1865Abolished slavery (except as punishment for a crime)
14th1868Citizenship for all born or naturalized here; no state may deny due process or equal protection
15th1870Vote not denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude"

Promise vs. practice: poll taxes, literacy tests, violence, segregation → Plessy (1896) allowed "separate but equal" → Brown (1954) ended it in public schools → Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965)

notes.say: Right after the Civil War, three amendments changed the Constitution more than any since the Bill of Rights. The 13th ended slavery. The 14th made everyone born or naturalized in the United States a citizen, reversing the Dred Scott decision of 1857, and it told the states they may not deny any person due process or the equal protection of the laws. The 15th said the vote may not be denied because of race. Be honest about what came next: after Reconstruction, many states used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to keep Black citizens from voting, and passed segregation laws. In 1896 the Court allowed "separate but equal" in Plessy v. Ferguson. In 1954, Brown v. Board of Education ruled that segregated public schools violate equal protection. Congress then passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to enforce these promises.
ask: Which amendment did Brown v. Board of Education rely on? (Expected: the 14th, the equal protection clause)
Why was the Voting Rights Act needed if the 15th Amendment existed since 1870? (Expected: states used poll taxes, literacy tests, and intimidation to get around it)
notes.watch: Students often say the 14th Amendment ended slavery. Use the order: 13 ends slavery, 14 makes citizens and promises equal protection, 15 protects the vote from race discrimination.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Opinions, 58 Years Apart
slides.board:
A: Justice Harlan, dissenting in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): "Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens."

B: Chief Justice Warren for a unanimous Court, Brown v. Board of Education (1954): "Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."

How are the two related?
steps: Step 1: Identify each source. A is a dissent: Harlan disagreed with the majority, which allowed segregated rail cars. A dissent is not law.
Step 2: Identify each claim. A: the Constitution should not divide citizens by race. B: separate schools are unequal.
Step 3: Connect them. 1954 − 1896 = 58 years. The Court in B reached, for public schools, the view Harlan argued alone in A.
Answer: Brown agreed with Harlan’s dissent and rejected "separate but equal" in public education.

notes.say: This is a classic paired-source question. Teach the student to label each source before reading the claim: who wrote it, when, and was it the majority or a dissent? That label alone eliminates the most tempting wrong answer, which says Harlan's opinion overturned Plessy. A dissent has no legal force, though it can influence later courts.
ask: What is a dissent? (Expected: an opinion written by a justice who disagrees with the majority; it is not law)
notes.watch: If the student says "Excerpt A overturned Plessy," ask: "Was Harlan in the majority?" Only a later majority decision can overturn a ruling.

slides.title: We Do: Which Amendment Changed This?
slides.board:
1. Before 1868, the Supreme Court had said Black Americans could not be U.S. citizens. What changed that?
  2. A state refuses to count ballots from Black voters. Which amendment does this violate?
  3. A state school system sends students to different schools by race. Which clause did Brown use to strike this down?
steps: 1. The 14th Amendment (1868): "All persons born or naturalized in the United States… are citizens." This reversed Dred Scott (1857).
2. The 15th Amendment (1870): the vote may not be denied "on account of race."
3. The equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment: no state may "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws."

notes.say: Have the student answer each with the amendment and the phrase that proves it. These three questions match the three most-tested ideas from the Civil War amendments: citizenship, the vote, and equal protection.
ask: Which word in the 14th Amendment shows it protects more than citizens? (Expected: "any person")
notes.answer: 1. 14th Amendment, citizenship clause. 2. 15th Amendment. 3. Equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.
notes.watch: Students may answer number 2 with the 14th Amendment because it promises equal protection. That is not wrong as a general idea, but the 15th Amendment names voting and race directly, so it is the best answer.

slides.title: Expanding the Vote and Article V
slides.board:
AmendmentYearWhat it did
15th1870No denying the vote because of race
17th1913Voters elect U.S. senators directly
19th1920No denying the vote because of sex
24th1964No poll taxes in federal elections
26th1971Citizens 18 and older: no denying the vote because of age

Memory hook: 15 = race, 19 = women, 26 = age 18.
Article V: propose by 2/3 of both houses → ratify by 3/4 of states (38 of 50).

notes.say: Over time, amendments widened who can vote. The 15th banned race discrimination in voting. The 17th let voters, not state legislatures, choose U.S. senators. The 19th, in 1920, banned denying the vote because of sex. The 24th, in 1964, banned poll taxes in federal elections. The 26th, in 1971, guaranteed the vote to citizens 18 and older; it was ratified in about 100 days during the Vietnam War, when young people argued that anyone old enough to be drafted was old enough to vote. Every one of these needed the Article V process: two-thirds of both houses to propose, three-fourths of the states to ratify. That high bar is why there are only 27 amendments.
ask: Which amendment guaranteed women the right to vote, and when? (Expected: the 19th, 1920)
How many states must ratify an amendment today? (Expected: 38, three-fourths of 50)
notes.watch: The 17th Amendment did not give anyone the right to vote for the first time; it changed how senators are chosen. Students who say "the 17th let women vote" are mixing it up with the 19th.

slides.title: Worked Example: Does the Amendment Pass?
slides.board:
All 435 representatives and all 100 senators vote on a proposed amendment.

  • House: 301 yes, 134 no
  • Senate: 65 yes, 35 no

Is the amendment proposed to the states? If not, how many more Senate yes votes were needed?
steps: House: 2/3 × 435 = 290. 301 ≥ 290, so the House approves.
Senate: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67. You cannot have part of a senator, so round up to 67.
Compare: 65 < 67, so the Senate falls short. Both houses must reach two-thirds.
Answer: Not proposed. It needed 67 − 65 = 2 more Senate yes votes.

notes.say: The GED sometimes asks you to do this kind of count. The three habits: multiply by the fraction, round up whenever the result is not a whole number (66 senators would be less than two-thirds), and remember that both houses must pass it. If it had been proposed, it would still need 38 states.
ask: Why round 66.67 up instead of down? (Expected: 66 is less than two-thirds of 100; you need at least two-thirds)
If the amendment were proposed, how many states would have to ratify it? (Expected: 38)
notes.watch: Students who round to the nearest whole number get 67 here, but they will miss cases like 2/3 of 98 = 65.33, where the answer is 66, not 65. Teach "round up" as the rule.

slides.title: We Do: Voting Amendments
slides.board:
1. In 1910, which body chose U.S. senators? Which amendment changed this?
  2. In 1962, a voter had to pay $2 before voting for a member of Congress. Which amendment later banned that?
  3. A proposed amendment has been ratified by 33 states. How many more states are needed?
steps: 1. State legislatures chose senators; the 17th Amendment (1913) gave that choice to voters.
2. That fee was a poll tax; the 24th Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections.
3. 3/4 × 50 = 37.5, so round up to 38. 38 − 33 = 5 more states.

notes.say: Work these together. Number 1 connects back to last week: the original Constitution had state legislatures choose senators. Number 3 uses the same round-up rule as the last slide.
ask: Why is the answer to number 3 not 4.5? (Expected: you cannot ratify with half a state; three-fourths of 50 is 37.5, so 38 states are needed)
notes.answer: 1. State legislatures; 17th Amendment. 2. 24th Amendment. 3. 5 more states.
notes.watch: On number 3, some students subtract from 50 (17). Ask: "Do we need all 50, or three-fourths of them?"

slides.title: Citizenship: Paths, Rights, Responsibilities
slides.board:
Two paths: birth (in the U.S., or in some cases abroad to a citizen parent) or naturalization (generally 18+, usually 5 years as a permanent resident or 3 if married to and living with a citizen, good moral character, English and civics tests, Oath of Allegiance)

Required by law
Obey laws · Pay taxes · Jury service when summoned · Selective Service (most men 18–25)

Voluntary but important
Vote · Stay informed · Volunteer · Contact officials

Citizens only: vote in federal elections, serve on a federal jury, hold most federal offices. Most other rights protect every person.

notes.say: There are two ways to become a U.S. citizen. Most people are citizens by birth, under the 14th Amendment. Others become citizens through naturalization: generally they must be at least 18, usually have five years as a lawful permanent resident (three if married to and living with a U.S. citizen), show good moral character, pass English and civics tests, and take the Oath of Allegiance. Citizenship brings responsibilities. Some are required by law: obey laws, pay taxes, serve on a jury when summoned, and for most men ages 18 through 25, register with the Selective Service System. Others are voluntary but important: voting, staying informed, volunteering. A few rights belong only to citizens, such as voting in federal elections. But most constitutional rights, such as free speech, due process, and equal protection, protect every person in the country.
ask: Is voting required by federal law? (Expected: No; it is a right and a voluntary responsibility)
Name a right that protects every person, not just citizens. (Expected: free speech, due process, equal protection, a fair trial, and so on)
notes.watch: The most common error is calling voting a legal requirement. Use the test: "Can you be legally penalized for not doing it?" You can for ignoring a jury summons; you cannot for skipping an election.

slides.title: Worked Example: Required or Voluntary?
slides.board:
Sort each activity: required by law or voluntary?

  1. Paying federal income tax
  2. Voting in a city election
  3. Serving on a jury after receiving a summons
  4. Writing a letter to a senator
steps: The test: Can a person be legally penalized for not doing it?
Required: (1) taxes and (3) jury service after a summons. Ignoring either can bring legal penalties.
Voluntary: (2) voting and (4) contacting a senator. Both matter, but no federal law requires them.
Answer: Required: 1 and 3. Voluntary: 2 and 4.

notes.say: Teach the one-question test and let it do the work. Point out that voluntary does not mean unimportant: voting is both a right and a civic responsibility. The GED likes drag-and-drop items that sort exactly these activities.
ask: Where would "registering with the Selective Service at age 18" go for most men? (Expected: required by law)
notes.watch: Students sometimes put jury service under voluntary because many people try to get out of it. The summons is a legal order; ignoring it can bring penalties.

slides.title: Reading Civics Data
slides.board:
Routine: read the title, labels, and units → write down the exact values → calculate → check the claim.

Age group18–2425–4445–6465+
Reported voting41%55%66%72%
  • Percentage points: subtract. 72 − 41 = 31 points.
  • A chart shows what, not why. It cannot prove a cause.
  • "Most" means more than 50%.

notes.say: Civics questions often come with a chart about voting or civic life. Use last week's routine: title, labels, units, exact values. Then judge each answer choice against the numbers. The difference between two percents is in percentage points: subtract. And remember the biggest trap: a chart tells you what happened, not why. If an answer says a law or an amendment "caused" a number, the chart alone cannot prove it.
ask: In this table, did a majority of 18–24-year-olds report voting? (Expected: No, 41% is less than half)
Can this table tell us why older people voted more? (Expected: No; it shows rates, not reasons)
notes.watch: Students who know the 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18 may choose an answer that says the amendment "caused" young people to vote less. Ask: "Where in the chart is the cause?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Before and After a Law
slides.board:
Fictional Carver County: percent of eligible Black adults registered to vote.

1960196419661968
5%7%38%55%

The Voting Rights Act passed in August 1965.

(a) Find the change from 1964 to 1968. (b) Does the table prove the act caused the change?
steps: (a) Values: 1964 = 7%, 1968 = 55%.
Subtract: 55 − 7 = 48 percentage points.
(b) Check the claim: The big jump comes after 1965, which fits the act’s purpose. But the table shows only timing; other events could also matter.
Answer: (a) 48 percentage points. (b) No. The data are consistent with the act having an effect, but they do not prove it alone.

notes.say: Teach the difference between "supports" and "proves." A GED answer that says the rise happened after the act is supported. An answer that says the act alone caused all of the rise goes too far. Note also that 1968 is the first year a majority was registered: 55% is more than half.
ask: In which year did a majority first register? (Expected: 1968, 55%)
notes.watch: Some students write "48%." Correct it: the difference between two percents is 48 percentage points.

slides.title: You Do 1: The Bill of Rights
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Who drafted the Bill of Rights, and in what year were the ten amendments ratified?
  2. A city arrests protesters who are marching peacefully on a public sidewalk. Which First Amendment freedom is most involved?
  3. Police listen to a suspect’s confession after forcing him to talk with threats. Which amendment protects him?
  4. A judge sets bail at $1 million for a person accused of shoplifting a $20 shirt. Which amendment?
steps: 1. James Madison; 1791. 2. Assembly (peaceably to assemble). 3. The 5th (no forced self-incrimination). 4. The 8th (no excessive bail).

notes.say: Three minutes, quiet, then the student reports each answer and names the clue word. Do not reveal until all four are given. Praise the reasoning: "Forced to talk, so self-incrimination, so the Fifth."
notes.watch: On number 2, students may say speech. Marching together is a gathering, so assembly is the most specific match. Accept speech as related, but ask for the better answer.

slides.title: You Do 2: Rights and Equal Protection
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Liberty or right? A landlord refuses to rent to a family because of their race.
  2. Which amendment abolished slavery, and in what year?
  3. Which two clauses of the 14th Amendment protect "any person," not only citizens?
  4. What does it mean that the Bill of Rights was "incorporated"?
steps: 1. Civil right. 2. The 13th, 1865. 3. Due process and equal protection. 4. The Court used the 14th Amendment to apply most Bill of Rights protections to state and local governments.

notes.say: Same routine. For number 4, require the student to name the 14th Amendment and to say "states" in the answer. Incorporation is a frequent source of confusion, so check it carefully.
notes.answer: 1. Civil right. 2. 13th, 1865. 3. Due process clause and equal protection clause. 4. Most protections now limit state and local governments too, through the 14th Amendment.
notes.watch: If the student says incorporation means "added to the Constitution," correct it: nothing new was added; the Court applied existing protections to the states.

slides.title: You Do 3: The Vote, Citizenship, and Data
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18, and why was it popular during the Vietnam War?
  2. Required or voluntary: (a) obeying traffic laws (b) volunteering at a shelter (c) serving on a jury after a summons
  3. Turnout: 18–24 = 41%, 65+ = 72%. How many percentage points higher was the 65+ group?
steps: 1. The 26th (1971); people argued that anyone old enough to be drafted was old enough to vote. 2. (a) required (b) voluntary (c) required. 3. 72 − 41 = 31 percentage points.

notes.say: Four minutes for this one because of the calculation. When the student reports number 3, ask them to say the unit out loud: percentage points.
notes.answer: 1. 26th Amendment (1971); draft-age argument. 2. (a) required (b) voluntary (c) required. 3. 31 percentage points.
notes.watch: If the student answers "31%," remind them: subtracting two percents gives percentage points.

slides.title: GED Question 1: A Court Opinion
slides.board:
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963): "in our adversary system of criminal justice, any person haled into court, who is too poor to hire a lawyer, cannot be assured a fair trial unless counsel is provided for him."

Which situation would the Court most likely find unconstitutional under this reasoning?

A. A wealthy defendant hires a well-known private lawyer for a murder trial.
B. A defendant who cannot afford a lawyer is tried for a felony with no lawyer.
C. A defendant chooses to plead guilty to a parking ticket without a lawyer.
D. A defendant’s court-appointed lawyer loses the case at trial.
steps: Eliminate A. The rule is about people "too poor to hire a lawyer." This defendant has a lawyer, so no right is denied.
Eliminate C. A parking ticket is not a criminal trial for a serious crime, and the person chose to go without a lawyer.
Eliminate D. The opinion guarantees a lawyer, not a win. Losing with an appointed lawyer is not denial of counsel.

Answer B. A poor defendant tried for a felony with no lawyer is exactly the person the Court says "cannot be assured a fair trial." This is the 6th Amendment right to counsel, applied to the states through the 14th.

notes.say: Read the excerpt with the student and translate it first: "If you are too poor to hire a lawyer, the court must provide one, or the trial is not fair." Then test each choice against that rule. Each wrong answer here is a type: A has no problem at all, C is outside the rule, and D confuses a right to a lawyer with a right to win.
ask: What does "counsel" mean here? (Expected: a lawyer)
Which amendment contains the right to counsel? (Expected: the 6th)
notes.answer: B. A defendant too poor to hire a lawyer is tried for a felony without one.
notes.watch: D is the trap for students who think "unfair outcome" equals "unconstitutional." Ask: "What exactly does the opinion promise?"

slides.title: GED Question 2: Reading a Chart
slides.board:
Fictional Harmon: percent of eligible residents who reported voting.

18–2425–4445–6465+
41%55%66%72%

Which statement is supported by the data?

A. Most residents aged 18–24 reported voting.
B. The 26th Amendment caused young residents to vote less often.
C. Each older age group reported voting at a higher rate than the group before it.
D. More residents aged 65 and older voted than residents of any other age.
steps: Eliminate A. 41% is less than half. "Most" needs more than 50%.
Eliminate B. The chart shows rates, not causes. Nothing in it is about the 26th Amendment.
Eliminate D. The chart shows percents of each group, not the number of voters. A larger group with a lower rate could have more voters.
Answer C. 41 < 55 < 66 < 72: each older group is higher than the one before it.

notes.say: D is the most sophisticated trap on this slide: it turns a rate into a count. Spend a moment on it. If the 25–44 group has three times as many people as the 65+ group, 55% of them is far more voters than 72% of the smaller group. Rates and counts are different measures.
ask: What would you need to know to decide which group had the most voters? (Expected: the number of residents in each group)
notes.answer: C. Each older group reported voting at a higher rate than the group before it.
notes.watch: Students who pick B are usually using outside knowledge. Ask: "Does the chart mention the amendment anywhere?"

slides.title: GED Strategy: Translate the Scenario First
slides.board:
1. Say what is happening in plain words: searching, silencing, punishing, refusing service, denying a vote.
  2. Ask who is acting. Government limiting a freedom → civil liberty. A group treated unequally → civil right.
  3. Find the stage for criminal cases: search (4th) → charges and questioning (5th) → trial (6th) → punishment (8th).
  4. Match the most specific amendment or phrase.
  5. Prove it with the words of the excerpt.

Pace: about 2 minutes per question.

notes.say: Most rights questions on the GED are scenario questions. The fastest, most accurate way through them is to translate the scenario into one plain verb before you look at the options. Once the student says "the police searched" or "the state refused the vote because of age," the matching amendment is usually obvious, and the distractors, which name related but less specific rights, fall away.
ask: A state charges a $10 fee to vote for Congress. Translate it into plain words, then name the amendment. (Expected: "charging people to vote"; the 24th)
notes.watch: Strong students sometimes pick the broadest right, such as due process, for everything. Remind them that the GED rewards the most specific match.

slides.title: Recap and Next Steps
slides.board:
• Bill of Rights (1791, Madison) limits government. 1st = religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.
  • Accused: search (4th) → charges (5th) → trial (6th) → punishment (8th).
  • Liberties = freedom from government; rights = equal treatment. Rights have limits.
  • 13th ends slavery, 14th citizenship + due process + equal protection, 15th race and the vote. 19 = women, 24 = poll tax, 26 = age 18.
  • Citizenship: birth or naturalization; taxes and jury duty required; voting voluntary.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

notes.say: Have the student state each takeaway in their own words before you reveal the next. Then set up the week: the Student Lesson walks through every idea again with a check on each screen, the Practice has 15 GED-style questions (and a second set if they score under 80 percent), and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for Week 4, where we study elections, political parties, and public policy.
ask: Which amendment number do you find hardest to remember? (Expected: any answer; give the student one memory hook for it, such as "15 = race, 19 = women, 26 = age 18")

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
Questions about rights show up all through the GED Social Studies test. You will often read a short piece of an amendment or a Supreme Court opinion, then decide what it protects or how it applies to a situation. This lesson teaches the amendments that matter most and gives you a method for matching any situation to the right that covers it.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain why the Bill of Rights was added and name the main protection in each of the first ten amendments
  • Tell civil liberties from civil rights and explain why rights have limits
  • Describe how the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments changed the Constitution, and how later amendments expanded the vote
  • Explain how a person becomes a citizen and sort citizens’ duties into required and voluntary
  • Answer GED-style questions using amendment texts, court opinions, tables, and charts

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: Why a Bill of Rights?
screens.html:
When the Constitution was written in 1787, it created a strong national government but listed very few individual rights. A group called the Anti-Federalists worried that this new government could become powerful enough to take away people’s freedoms. To win their support, supporters of the Constitution promised to add a list of rights.

James Madison drafted the amendments in 1789. Congress sent twelve to the states, and ten were ratified in 1791. These first ten amendments are the Bill of Rights.

Key idea: The Bill of Rights limits what the government can do to you. The First Amendment begins, "Congress shall make no law…"

check.skill: Purpose of the Bill of Rights
check.prompt: Why did the Anti-Federalists want a Bill of Rights added to the Constitution?
options: They feared the new national government could become strong enough to take away freedoms.
They wanted the national government to have more power over the states and their courts.
They wanted to create the three branches of government and divide power among them.
They believed a list of rights would let Congress pass laws more quickly and easily.
why: This is the opposite of their view. Anti-Federalists feared a strong national government; they did not want to give it more power.
The Constitution itself created the three branches in Articles I, II, and III. The Bill of Rights was added afterward to protect individual freedoms.
The Bill of Rights limits what Congress can do ("Congress shall make no law…"). It does not speed up lawmaking.
check.hint: Think about what they were afraid the new government might do.
check.explain: The Anti-Federalists feared that the stronger national government created by the Constitution would take away individual freedoms. Supporters promised a list of rights to win ratification, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The branches were already created by the Constitution, so that choice describes a different document.

screens.title: The First Amendment: Five Freedoms
screens.html:
The First Amendment protects five freedoms. Here is its full text:

"Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances."

FreedomIn plain words
ReligionNo official government church (establishment); people may practice their faith (free exercise)
SpeechExpress your ideas, including by symbols such as armbands
PressPublish news and opinions
AssemblyGather peacefully
PetitionFormally ask the government to fix a problem ("redress of grievances")

example.prompt: Neighbors collect signatures asking the county to repair a dangerous bridge, then deliver them to the county board. Which freedom protects them?
steps: Translate: they are formally asking the government to fix a problem.
Match: "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances."

check.prompt: About 200 people gather peacefully in a city park to show support for a new library. Which First Amendment freedom most directly protects this gathering?
options: Freedom of the press
The right to petition the government
The right to assemble
The free exercise of religion
why: Freedom of the press protects publishing news and opinions. These people are gathering, not publishing.
A petition is a formal request to the government. The people are gathering to show support, not delivering a request.
Free exercise protects practicing a religion. Nothing in this gathering is religious.
check.hint: Which freedom is about people coming together in one place?
check.explain: The First Amendment protects "the right of the people peaceably to assemble." A peaceful gathering in a park is assembly. Petition is the closest wrong answer, but a petition is a formal request to the government, and these people are simply gathering.

screens.title: The Search and the Charges: 4th and 5th Amendments
screens.html:
Four amendments protect people accused of crimes. The easiest way to remember them is to follow a case in order. The first two stages are the search and the charges.

4th Amendment: the search. The government may not make unreasonable searches and seizures. Usually police need a warrant, which a judge issues only when there is probable cause: a fact-based reason to believe a crime happened or evidence will be found.

5th Amendment: charges and questioning. It requires a grand jury for serious federal crimes and contains three key "no" rules:

  • No double jeopardy: you cannot be tried again for the same crime after a verdict.
  • No forced self-incrimination: you cannot be forced to testify against yourself ("pleading the Fifth").
  • No loss of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. It also requires fair payment when the government takes private property for public use.

example.prompt: A man is found not guilty of robbery. A month later, the prosecutor charges him with the same robbery again. Which amendment protects him?
steps: Translate: he is being tried a second time for the same crime after a verdict.
That is double jeopardy, which the 5th Amendment forbids.

check.prompt: Police want to search a woman’s apartment. A judge refuses to issue a warrant because the police have no probable cause. Which amendment requires probable cause for a warrant? Type the amendment number.

mistakes.why: The 5th Amendment covers charges and questioning (double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process). Searches and warrants are covered by the 4th.
The 6th Amendment covers the trial: a speedy, public trial, a jury, and a lawyer. A search comes earlier and is covered by the 4th.

check.hint: Follow the case in order: search, charges, trial, punishment.
check.explain: The 4th Amendment forbids unreasonable searches and seizures and says warrants may be issued only "upon probable cause." The search is the first stage of a case, so it is the first of the four criminal-justice amendments.

screens.title: The Trial and the Punishment: 6th, 7th, and 8th
screens.html:
6th Amendment: the trial. In a criminal case, the accused has the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury, to be told the charges, to confront (face and question) the witnesses against them, to call their own witnesses, and to have the help of a lawyer.

7th Amendment: a jury trial in many civil lawsuits, which are disputes between people or businesses rather than criminal charges.

8th Amendment: the punishment. "Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted." Bail is money paid to be released from jail while waiting for trial.

Memory trick: search (4th) → charges and questioning (5th) → trial (6th) → punishment (8th).

check.prompt: A man has been held in jail for two years, still waiting for his trial to begin, even though he has asked for one. Which amendment’s guarantee is most likely being violated? Type the amendment number.

mistakes.why: Due process (5th) is broad, but the 6th Amendment names this exact right: "a speedy and public trial." Always choose the most specific match.
The 8th Amendment covers bail, fines, and punishment. This man has not been convicted or sentenced; he is waiting for a trial, which is the 6th.

check.hint: Which amendment covers the trial stage?
check.explain: The 6th Amendment guarantees "a speedy and public trial." Two years of waiting after asking for a trial is the problem here. The 5th Amendment’s due process clause is related but less specific.

screens.title: The Rest of the Bill of Rights
screens.html:
You do not need to memorize every word of the Bill of Rights, but you should recognize the main idea of each amendment.

AmendmentMain idea
2ndThe right of the people to keep and bear arms
3rdNo soldiers housed in private homes in peacetime without the owner’s consent
9thListing some rights does not mean the people lack other rights
10thPowers not given to the national government, and not denied to the states, are reserved to the states or the people

The 10th Amendment connects to federalism from Week 2: it is the source of the reserved powers of the states, such as running schools and issuing driver’s licenses.

check.prompt: A state, not the national government, decides the requirements for getting a driver’s license. Which amendment supports the state’s power to make this decision?
options: The 9th Amendment, which says listing some rights does not take away others the people keep
The 1st Amendment, which protects speech, press, religion, assembly, and petition
The 3rd Amendment, which limits housing soldiers in private homes during peacetime
The 10th Amendment, which reserves powers not given to the nation to the states or people
why: The 9th Amendment is about rights the people keep, not powers the states hold. Reserved state powers come from the 10th.
The 1st Amendment protects individual freedoms. It says nothing about which level of government issues licenses.
The 3rd Amendment is only about quartering soldiers. It has nothing to do with state powers over licensing.
check.hint: This amendment is where the term "reserved powers" comes from.
check.explain: The 10th Amendment says powers not delegated to the national government, nor denied to the states, "are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." Licensing drivers is one of these reserved powers. The 9th is the tempting wrong answer because it is the neighbor of the 10th and also mentions "the people," but it is about unlisted rights, not state powers.

screens.title: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights
screens.html:
These two terms sound almost the same, but the GED expects you to tell them apart.

Civil liberties are basic freedoms the government may not take away: speech, religion, the press, privacy from unreasonable searches, a fair trial. Think: freedom from government interference.

Civil rights are guarantees of equal treatment, so people are not discriminated against because of race, sex, religion, national origin, or similar traits. Think: equal treatment under the law.

Ask one question: Is the government limiting a freedom, or is a group being treated unequally? The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination in public places such as hotels and restaurants and banned job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

example.prompt: A company refuses to hire qualified applicants because they are women. Is this a civil liberties issue or a civil rights issue?
steps: Ask: is a freedom being limited, or is a group being treated unequally? A group is treated unequally because of sex.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 bans job discrimination based on sex.

check.prompt: Which situation is mainly a civil liberties issue?
options: A store refuses to serve customers because of the country they were born in.
A city orders a newspaper to stop printing articles critical of the mayor.
A landlord refuses to rent apartments to families because of their religion.
A company pays women less than men for doing exactly the same work.
why: A store treating customers unequally because of national origin is a civil rights issue: unequal treatment of a group.
This involves religion, but the landlord is treating a group unequally, not limiting worship. That makes it a civil rights issue.
Unequal pay based on sex is unequal treatment of a group, which is a civil rights issue.
check.hint: Look for the one where the government itself is limiting a freedom.
check.explain: When the city orders a newspaper to stop criticizing the mayor, the government is limiting a freedom (freedom of the press). That is a civil liberties issue. The other three describe a group being treated unequally because of national origin, religion, or sex, which are civil rights issues. The religion choice is the most tempting trap: religion is mentioned, but the problem is unequal treatment, not a limit on worship.

screens.title: Rights Have Limits
screens.html:
Constitutional rights are strong, but they are not unlimited. Courts balance a person’s freedom against public safety and the rights of others.

  • The First Amendment does not protect true threats.
  • In Schenck v. United States (1919), the Supreme Court allowed punishment of speech that created a "clear and present danger." Later cases narrowed that test, so today far more speech is protected.
  • In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), students wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War. The Court ruled 7–2 that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." But a school may limit speech if it can show the speech would "materially and substantially interfere" with school discipline.

Notice that the armbands were not spoken or written. Speech includes symbolic expression.

check.prompt: Based on Tinker v. Des Moines, which school rule would most likely be upheld by a court?
options: A rule banning all political buttons, though no button has ever caused a problem at the school
A rule banning a protest that officials show has already caused fights and canceled classes
A rule banning armbands because some teachers dislike the opinion that the armbands express
A rule banning students from wearing any symbol about current events while on school grounds
why: Tinker says a ban "cannot be sustained" without a showing of substantial disruption. A ban with no problems at all fits the case the Court struck down.
Disliking an opinion is not a substantial disruption. Tinker protected students against exactly this kind of ban.
A blanket ban on symbols, with no evidence of disruption, is like the armband ban the Court rejected in Tinker.
check.hint: What must a school show before it can limit student speech?
check.explain: Tinker lets a school limit speech only when it can show the speech would "materially and substantially interfere" with school. A protest that has already led to fights and canceled classes meets that test, so that rule would most likely be upheld. The other three rules ban expression with no showing of disruption, which is what the Court rejected.

screens.title: Incorporation: Rights Against the States
screens.html:
When the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791, it limited only the national government. A state government was not bound by it.

That changed after the 14th Amendment (1868), which says no state may deprive any person of life, liberty, or property "without due process of law." Beginning in the 1920s, the Supreme Court used this due process clause to apply most of the Bill of Rights to state and local governments, one right at a time. This process is called incorporation.

  • Gideon v. Wainwright (1963): states must provide a lawyer to a person charged with a felony who cannot afford one.
  • Miranda v. Arizona (1966): before questioning a suspect in custody, police must warn the suspect of the right to remain silent and the right to a lawyer.

Because of incorporation, a city police officer, not just a federal agent, must respect your 4th Amendment rights.

check.prompt:
Complete the statement.

At first, the Bill of Rights limited only {{0}}. The Supreme Court later used the {{1}} to apply most of its protections to state and local governments.

options: the national government
state governments
private businesses
city governments
why: States were not bound by the Bill of Rights at first. Applying it to the states is what incorporation later did.
The Bill of Rights limits government, not private businesses. Business discrimination is covered by laws such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Cities are part of state and local government, which the Bill of Rights did not limit until incorporation.

options: 14th Amendment’s due process clause
10th Amendment’s reserved powers
15th Amendment’s voting protections
Constitution’s Supremacy Clause
why: The 10th Amendment reserves powers to the states; it does not limit them with the Bill of Rights.
The 15th Amendment is about voting and race. Incorporation used the 14th Amendment’s due process clause.
The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) makes federal law supreme, but the Court used the 14th Amendment’s due process clause for incorporation.

check.hint: Which amendment, written after the Civil War, begins its key rules with "No State shall"?
check.explain: In 1791 the Bill of Rights limited only the national government. After the 14th Amendment said no state may deny due process, the Court used the 14th Amendment’s due process clause to apply most of the Bill of Rights to the states. The 10th Amendment is a tempting wrong choice because it mentions states, but it reserves powers to them rather than limiting them.

screens.title: The Civil War Amendments
screens.html:
Right after the Civil War, three amendments changed the Constitution more than any since the Bill of Rights.

AmendmentYearWhat it did
13th1865Abolished slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for a crime
14th1868Made all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. citizens; no state may deny any person due process or equal protection of the laws
15th1870The vote may not be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude"

The 14th Amendment reversed Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), in which the Supreme Court had said Black Americans could not be U.S. citizens. Notice the words "any person" in the 14th Amendment: due process and equal protection cover everyone in a state, not just citizens.

example.prompt: Which Civil War amendment directly overturned the Dred Scott decision?
steps: Dred Scott was about who could be a citizen.
The 14th Amendment’s first sentence defines citizenship: "All persons born or naturalized in the United States… are citizens."

check.prompt: Drag each change into the amendment that made it.
choices: Ended slavery in the United States
Made everyone born in the United States a citizen
Banned denying the vote because of race
Required states to give every person equal protection of the laws
check.why: The most common mistake is putting "ended slavery" under the 14th. Remember the order: 13 ends slavery, 14 makes citizens and promises equal protection, 15 protects the vote from race discrimination.
check.hint: Two of the changes belong to the same amendment.
check.explain:
• 13th (1865): ended slavery.
  • 14th (1868): citizenship for all born or naturalized here, plus due process and equal protection. Two of the four statements belong here.
  • 15th (1870): no denying the vote on account of race.

screens.title: Promises Broken and Kept
screens.html:
The Civil War amendments made big promises, but they were often broken. After Reconstruction ended in 1877, many states used poll taxes (fees to vote), literacy tests, and violence to keep Black citizens from voting, and passed segregation ("Jim Crow") laws.

  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): the Court allowed "separate but equal" facilities. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, writing, "Our Constitution is color-blind." A dissent is the opinion of a justice who disagrees with the majority; it is not law.
  • Brown v. Board of Education (1954): a unanimous Court ruled that segregated public schools violate the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. "Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."
  • Civil Rights Act of 1964: outlawed segregation in public accommodations and job discrimination.
  • Voting Rights Act of 1965: targeted literacy tests and other practices used to deny the vote.

check.prompt: Click the sentence that describes a decision that was not law when it was written.
spans: In 1896, the majority in Plessy v. Ferguson allowed states to require separate railroad cars by race.
In the same case, Justice Harlan wrote alone that "Our Constitution is color-blind."
In 1954, a unanimous Court in Brown v. Board of Education ruled school segregation unconstitutional.
In 1964, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act, which outlawed segregation in public accommodations.
check.why: Many students click the Brown sentence because it is about ending segregation. But Brown was a majority decision, so it was law. Harlan’s opinion was a dissent.
check.hint: Which opinion was written by a justice who disagreed with the majority?
check.explain: Harlan’s opinion was a dissent: he disagreed with the majority, so his view had no legal force in 1896. The Plessy majority decision, the Brown decision, and the Civil Rights Act were all law when they were issued or passed. Harlan’s view was later echoed when Brown rejected "separate but equal" in public schools.

screens.title: Expanding the Right to Vote
screens.html:
Several amendments widened who can vote. Many of them use the same pattern: the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged" (reduced) "on account of" some trait.

AmendmentYearWhat it did
15th1870No denying the vote because of race
17th1913Voters, not state legislatures, elect U.S. senators
19th1920No denying the vote because of sex (women’s suffrage)
24th1964No poll taxes in federal elections
26th1971Citizens 18 or older may not be denied the vote because of age

The 26th Amendment was ratified in about 100 days during the Vietnam War, when young people argued that anyone old enough to be drafted was old enough to vote.

Memory hook: 15 = race, 19 = women, 26 = age 18.

check.prompt: Which amendment guaranteed that the right to vote may not be denied because of sex? Type the amendment number.

mistakes.why: The 15th Amendment (1870) protects the vote from denial because of race. The amendment about sex is the 19th (1920).
The 26th Amendment (1971) is about age: it protects citizens 18 and older. The amendment about sex is the 19th.

check.hint: Women won the vote nationwide in 1920.
check.explain: The 19th Amendment (1920) says the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged… on account of sex." Memory hook: 15 = race, 19 = women, 26 = age 18.

screens.title: How Amendments Are Added
screens.html:
Every amendment you have studied went through Article V of the Constitution. The usual path has two steps:

  1. Propose: two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote yes.
  2. Ratify: three-fourths of the states approve. With 50 states, that is 38.

When a fraction does not give a whole number, round up, because you cannot have part of a senator or a state. Two-thirds of 100 senators is 66.67, so 67 senators are needed. Three-fourths of 50 states is 37.5, so 38 states are needed.

This high bar is why there are only 27 amendments.

example.prompt: A proposed amendment has passed both houses of Congress and has been ratified by 30 states. How many more states must ratify it?
steps: States needed: 3/4 × 50 = 37.5, round up to 38.
More needed: 38 − 30 = 8.

check.prompt: All 435 members of the House vote on a proposed amendment. What is the fewest yes votes needed for the House to approve it?

mistakes.why: That is a simple majority (more than half of 435). Proposing an amendment takes two-thirds: 2/3 × 435 = 290.
You used three-fourths. Three-fourths is the fraction for ratification by the states. Congress proposes with two-thirds: 2/3 × 435 = 290.
That is one-third of 435. You need two-thirds: 2 × 145 = 290.

check.explain: Two-thirds of 435: 435 ÷ 3 = 145, and 145 × 2 = 290. This is a whole number, so no rounding is needed. A common mistake is using three-fourths, which is the fraction for the states, not for Congress.

screens.title: Becoming a Citizen
screens.html:
There are two paths to U.S. citizenship.

  • Birth: being born in the United States (under the 14th Amendment), or in some cases being born abroad to a parent who is a U.S. citizen.
  • Naturalization: the legal process by which an immigrant becomes a citizen. A person generally must be at least 18, usually have been a lawful permanent resident for five years (three years if married to and living with a U.S. citizen), show good moral character, pass English and civics tests, and take the Oath of Allegiance.

Some rights belong only to citizens: voting in federal elections, serving on a federal jury, and holding most federal offices. But most rights in the Constitution, such as free speech, due process, and equal protection, protect every person in the country, citizen or not.

options: The right to due process before losing liberty or property
The right to vote for a member of the U.S. Congress
The right to practice any religion or no religion at all
The right to equal protection under a state’s laws
why: The 5th and 14th Amendments protect "any person," citizen or not, from losing liberty or property without due process.
The First Amendment protects free exercise of religion for everyone in the country, not only citizens.
The 14th Amendment says no state may deny equal protection "to any person within its jurisdiction," so it is not limited to citizens.
check.hint: Most constitutional rights use the word "person." Which one is tied to citizenship?
check.explain: Voting in federal elections, such as for Congress, is limited to citizens. Due process, freedom of religion, and equal protection are protected for every person in the United States; the 14th Amendment uses the words "any person."

screens.title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizens
screens.html:
Citizenship comes with responsibilities. Some are required by law; others are voluntary but important for a democracy.

Required by law

  • Obey federal, state, and local laws
  • Pay taxes
  • Serve on a jury when summoned
  • Most men ages 18 through 25: register with the Selective Service System

Voluntary but important

  • Vote in elections
  • Stay informed about issues
  • Volunteer in the community
  • Contact elected officials

Test: Can a person be legally penalized for not doing it? If yes, it is required. Voting is both a right and a civic responsibility, but no federal law requires you to vote.

example.prompt: Is serving on a jury after receiving a summons required or voluntary?
steps: Ask: can a person be penalized for ignoring it? Yes, a summons is a legal order.
So jury service after a summons is required by law.

check.prompt: Drag each activity into the correct group.
choices: Paying federal income taxes
Voting in a state election
Serving on a jury after a summons
Volunteering at a food bank
Following traffic laws
check.why: The most common mistake is putting voting under "Required by law." Voting is important, but no federal law requires it; you cannot be penalized for not voting.
check.hint: Ask of each: can a person be legally penalized for not doing it?
check.explain:
Required: paying taxes, serving on a jury after a summons, and obeying laws such as traffic laws. Ignoring any of these can bring legal penalties.

Voluntary: voting and volunteering. Both matter, but no law requires them.

screens.title: Reading Civics Data
screens.html:
Many GED civics questions come with a chart about voting or civic life. Use this routine:

  1. Read the title, labels, and units.
  2. Write down the exact values you need.
  3. Calculate. The difference between two percents is in percentage points: subtract.
  4. Check each claim. A chart shows what happened, not why. "Most" means more than 50%. A rate (percent of a group) is not a count (number of people).

example.prompt: In a fictional county, 7% of eligible Black adults were registered to vote in 1964 and 55% in 1968. The Voting Rights Act passed in 1965. Find the change. Does the table prove the act caused it?
steps: Change: 55 − 7 = 48 percentage points.
The rise came after the act, which supports a connection, but the table shows only timing. It cannot prove the act was the only cause.
example.answer: 48 percentage points; the data support but do not prove a cause.

check.prompt: In a fictional town, 38% of residents aged 18–29 and 69% of residents aged 60 and older reported voting. How many percentage points higher was the rate for residents 60 and older?

mistakes.why: You added the two rates. To compare them, subtract: 69 − 38.
You found how much larger 69 is as a percent of 38 (31 ÷ 38). The question asks for percentage points, so just subtract: 69 − 38 = 31.

check.hint: Subtract the smaller rate from the larger rate.
check.explain: 69 − 38 = 31 percentage points. The difference between two percents is measured in percentage points, found by subtracting.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Bill of Rights (ratified 1791, drafted by Madison) limits the government. 1st: religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.
  • Criminal case order: search (4th) → charges and questioning (5th: double jeopardy, self-incrimination, due process) → trial (6th: speedy trial, jury, lawyer) → punishment (8th: bail, fines, cruel and unusual). 10th: reserved powers.
  • Civil liberties = freedom from government interference. Civil rights = equal treatment. Rights have limits (Tinker: substantial disruption).
  • Incorporation: the 14th Amendment’s due process clause applies most of the Bill of Rights to the states.
  • 13th (1865) ends slavery; 14th (1868) citizenship, due process, equal protection; 15th (1870) race and the vote. Plessy (1896) → Brown (1954).
  • Vote: 17th senators, 19th women, 24th poll taxes, 26th age 18. Amend: 2/3 of Congress, 3/4 of states (38). Round up.
  • Citizenship: birth or naturalization. Required: obey laws, taxes, jury service. Voluntary: voting, volunteering.
  • Data: subtract for percentage points; a chart shows what, not why.

Next: the Practice set. Read every explanation, even on questions you get right.

stimuli.title: Document 3: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969)
stimuli.html:
Background: In December 1965, several students in Des Moines, Iowa, wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. School officials had adopted a rule banning armbands a few days earlier, and the students who refused to remove them were suspended. The students’ families sued. On February 24, 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 in favor of the students. Justice Abe Fortas wrote for the majority:

"It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.…

Certainly where there is no finding and no showing that engaging in the forbidden conduct would 'materially and substantially interfere with the requirements of appropriate discipline in the operation of the school,' the prohibition cannot be sustained."
stimuli.source: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, 393 U.S. 503 (1969), opinion of the Court by Justice Abe Fortas

Excerpt B — Chief Justice Earl Warren, for a unanimous Court in Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
